catalog_quote: In Saxwe, there are three tonal heights which are the realization of a three-way underlying tonal contrast: /H, M, L/. Utterance-final /M/ and /L/ are both realized with the final downglide that is frequently seen on utterance-final /L/ in many African languages. [p. 63] ... The default tonal assignment for borrowed words is that the nucleus of a syllable that would normally bear primary stress in the original language is assigned H tone and the nuclei of all other syllables are assigned L tone. This is seen in the following examples. In all of these examples, primary stress (and therefore H tone) falls on a non-final syllable of the word. [pp. 180-181] ... When primary stress in the source language falls on the final syllable, the word in Saxwe is assigned a H tone associated to the TBU of the final syllable—following the same principle as with other borrowed words. new_statements.rule_in_words: Saxwe is a three-tone language (H, M, L underlying; mora is the tone-bearing unit; lexical tone on nouns and verbs plus grammatical tone, tonal spread, downstep and boundary tones). The 365-page tone monograph and the 2013 segmental phonology sketch contain no section on stress or accent and no claim that Saxwe has word stress; the only mention of stress is that English primary stress is reinterpreted as H tone when words are borrowed (other syllables L, or L/M), which implies tone rather than stress carries word-level prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: For loanwords: when source-language stress is word-final the Saxwe form has final H plus a floating M (p. 184, p. 237); some loans take M instead of L on unstressed syllables (p. 248, e.g. 'teacher' /tʃítʃā/ vs 'tailor' /télà/).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone on monomorphemic nouns (V.C(C)V) and verbs (C(C)V), with isolation forms carrying an utterance-final L% boundary; loanword rule is word-level.
new_statements.identity_note: Saxwe = Saxwɛgbe = Sahouè (ISO sxw, saxw1241), Glottolog: Gbe > Western Phla-Phera; Capo classes it in Phla-Phera, Kluge 2007 in Eastern Gbe. Beavon-Ham 2019 describes the variety of the Houeyogbe district (the [dṹtũ̀] subdivision; principal consultant from Adrome), and notes Lobogo/Bopa ([dàkplâ], incl. the lect called Gbokpa) subdivisions; Daxe and Se are the closest neighbouring varieties (Johnson 2011 treats them separately).

sources.note: Full tone study; sec. 3.1 p. 63: three-way underlying tonal contrast /H, M, L/; mora is the TBU (pp. 173, 192). No section on stress/accent; phonology overview (sec. 1.4, pp. 6-16) never mentions stress. The only stress statements concern English loanwords: the syllable bearing primary stress in the source language gets H tone, other syllables L (pp. 180-181, 184), 'stress being reinterpreted as H tone in Saxwe' (p. 192), final-stressed loans get final H plus floating M (p. 237).
